text.title: Product Development Trends Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules for a developer-tooling and practice trend scan: which adoption metrics count as evidence, why cumulative counters are banned, how hype phase must be sourced to a named maturity framework, and why every applicability verdict must price the exit as well as the entry.

rule.statement: Each `adoption_signals` entry MUST be a share over a stated practitioner or repository population, with the population, the date, and the source named — e.g. percent of respondents in the Stack Overflow Developer Survey or the JetBrains State of Developer Ecosystem, package-manager downloads as a fraction of the category total, or job postings mentioning the tool as a fraction of postings in the same stack. Vendor press releases, funding announcements and conference-talk counts are NOT adoption signals.

rationale.source: Stack Overflow Developer Survey / JetBrains State of Developer Ecosystem — share-of-respondents methodology

rule.rationale: Vendor announcements measure marketing spend, and a raw count with no denominator cannot distinguish a tool at 3% of its category from one at 40% — which is exactly the distinction the invest-or-wait decision turns on.

rule.statement: GitHub stars, all-time download totals, cumulative signups and total funding raised MUST NOT appear as adoption evidence. Use period-over-period rates instead: monthly download counts, weekly active dependent repositories, release cadence, issue-close latency.

rationale.source: Monotonic-metric failure in OSS health measurement (CHAOSS project metric guidance)

rule.rationale: A cumulative counter cannot decrease, so an abandoned project's star count keeps climbing from drive-by traffic long after its last release; the metric is structurally incapable of emitting the decline signal the scan exists to catch.

rule.statement: Each `hype_curve` phase MUST be justified by an external maturity assessment naming the framework and its edition — Gartner Hype Cycle with year, or Thoughtworks Technology Radar with ring (adopt / trial / assess / hold) and volume number — or by two independent adoption metrics moving in opposite directions. A self-assigned phase with neither is rejected.
rule.rationale: The phase is what drives the invest-now-or-wait call, and a self-assigned phase is fitted after the author has already decided; sourcing it to a dated external ring makes the call auditable and lets the next edition show whether the tool actually moved.

rule.statement: For every tooling trend record: release status (GA / beta / preview), whether a stable public API or config contract is published, the licence and any recent licence change, and the vendor's deprecation record for adjacent products.

rationale.source: Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 — pre-1.0 and pre-release contracts

rule.rationale: Pre-GA products explicitly disclaim compatibility, so breaking changes ship without a deprecation window; a team adopting at preview pays the integration cost twice — once now and again at GA — and that second payment usually exceeds the productivity gain the trend promised.

rule.statement: Each `applicability` entry MUST state the concrete adoption cost against THIS codebase (files or modules touched, CI/pipeline changes, editor or agent config, retraining) AND the exit path if abandoned within 12 months: is configuration and data exportable, does it alter build output or on-disk formats, is it a one-way door. Trends with no exit path are marked `hold` regardless of adoption score.

rationale.source: Internal — reversibility review on tooling adoption

rule.rationale: Dev tooling embeds into CI definitions, lockfiles, generated code and developer muscle memory, so the true cost is dominated by the reversal cost — a quantity that no adoption metric measures and that therefore never appears in a scan that scores popularity alone.

rule.statement: The scan MUST include at least one declining or end-of-life item already present in the team's stack, with its published support-end date and the migration target.

rationale.source: OSS support-lifecycle practice (Node.js LTS schedule, Python PEP 602 release cadence)

rule.rationale: A scan listing only rising things yields a to-add list with no to-remove list, but adoption capacity comes from retirement; meanwhile the unlisted unsupported dependency stops receiving security patches and reappears later as an audit finding rather than a planning item.

rule.statement: Do NOT run when (a) there is no budget or engineering capacity to change tooling this cycle — the scan produces a wish list; (b) the stack is frozen by a contractual or certification constraint; (c) the question is about a single named tool already chosen, which is an evaluation not a scan — route to a spike or a bake-off; (d) the team is under 6 months old and has not yet stabilised a baseline, so `applicability` has no codebase to price against.
rule.rationale: Without a baseline stack and the capacity to change it, `applicability` can only be filled with generic fit statements, and a trend scan whose applicability column is generic is indistinguishable from a vendor newsletter.
